title: Bechukotai: still remembered (Leviticus 26:42–45)
hookLine: even after the warnings, God remembers the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham

lines: AT THE BOTTOM, A DRAWER OPENS.
cards: There's a drawer in a lot of homes with old things nobody throws out: a hospital bracelet from a birth, a note in a grandparent's handwriting, a ring that doesn't fit anyone anymore.
The things in that drawer have outlived the quarrels around them. A family can fight for years, and the drawer still holds the proof that someone once promised to love someone.
The warnings in Leviticus twenty-six get very dark: an empty land, a scattered people. Then, right at the bottom, the chapter opens a drawer.

teach.b: After the exile, after the empty fields, God says: "then will I remember My covenant with Jacob, and also My covenant with Isaac, and also My covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land."
Listen to the order. Not Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the way the names usually run. It goes backwards.
Rashi offers a reading: it's as if God reaches back one generation at a time. Jacob alone would be reason enough; and if not, there's Isaac with him; and if not, Abraham.
The memory keeps reaching further back until it finds enough. Verse forty-four says what remembering means in practice.
Even when they're in the land of their enemies, God will not reject them, nor abhor them so as to destroy them utterly, and break the covenant.

teach.h: THE WARNINGS STAND. MEMORY ENDS IT.
teach.b: And verse forty-five adds one more memory: the covenant with the generation brought out of Egypt. Notice what the chapter doesn't do. It doesn't cancel the warnings or pretend they weren't said.
But the chapter closes on memory, a promise older than the failure, held by the one who made it. The relationship can be strained to breaking. Verse forty-four says it isn't broken.

how: When the warnings of Leviticus 26 are read in many synagogues, the reader's voice returns to full strength for the closing verses of remembrance; the theme of God remembering the covenant with the ancestors runs through Jewish prayer, especially on Rosh Hashanah.

o: in My statutes: Leviticus's final portion
the covenant made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
the memory of the people's exodus from Egypt

games.q: the drawer at the bottom — tap the pairs.

s: it ends with God remembering the covenant and the land.
the patriarchs are named in reverse order in verse 42
Jacob, then Isaac, then Abraham; Rashi reads it as memory reaching further back.
the closing verses cancel the warnings
the warnings stand; the closing verses say they aren't the end.

games.q: the warnings have described an empty land and a scattered people. what comes next in the chapter?
o: God remembers the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham.
games.why: "then will I remember My covenant." even in the land of their enemies, God says, they will not be rejected.

practice: Go back through the years slowly, the way the verse goes back through the generations, and find one promise once made to you: a parent who said I'll always come get you, a teacher who said you can do this, a friend who said call me, any hour.
Remember the voice, the room, the moment. Notice that the promise still exists, even if the person is far away, or gone, or changed.

wordCard.voice: Bechukotai, Leviticus's last portion. After the blessings and the warnings, it ends with God remembering: the covenant, the ancestors, and the land.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I will remember My covenant. zachar, remember; brit, covenant.

carryVoice: Your line: still remembered. The warnings stand, and the promise is older. Day four hundred twenty-eight.
